clue.text: Jet-smart for town

parts.note: jet is a deep glossy black, so jet as a colour means black
to smart is to sting or burn with pain

explanation.surface: Someone fashionable enough to be called jet-smart, hunting for a town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jet-smart' looks like one hyphenated adjective; split it into two words. BLACKBURN is a town in Lancashire, in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Blackburn is a Lancashire mill town, an example of the category named.

clue.text: Lights exterior of gold carriages

indicators.note: being the exterior of something means wrapping around it, so the first piece encloses the second

parts.note: a bird lights, or lands, on a branch: both mean comes down to settle
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: Gleaming lamps on the outside of gilded coaches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lights' reads as a noun (lamps) but is the verb 'alights', giving LANDS, which wraps round AU.
explanation.definitionFit: A landau is a four-wheeled horse-drawn coach with a folding hood, so the plural names such vehicles.

clue.text: The small farmer is allowed credit frequently with little hesitation

parts.note: CR is the usual abbreviation for credit in accounts
oft is an old word for often, frequently
er is the small sound of someone hesitating in speech

explanation.surface: A smallholder who is often given credit by a bank that barely hesitates.
explanation.walkthrough: A CROFTER works a croft, a small rented farm, chiefly in the Scottish Highlands.
explanation.definitionFit: A crofter rents and works a croft, a small agricultural holding, chiefly in Scotland.

clue.text: Old husband incarcerated in vile prison

indicators.note: something locked up in another is put inside it, so the second piece goes within the first

parts.note: base means low, mean, vile
to husband land in its old sense is to cultivate or till it

explanation.surface: An elderly married man locked up in a horrible jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Husband' reads as a married man but is the old farming verb, to till. TILL goes inside BASE as BAS-TILL-E, the Paris fortress-prison stormed in 1789.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bastille was a notorious state jail in Paris, a famous historic example of a place of confinement.

clue.text: The head girl's spice

parts.note: nut is slang for the head
Meg is a girl's name, the possessive linking it to what follows

explanation.surface: A headmistress or head girl's favourite seasoning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The head girl' looks like a school prefect, but the phrase splits into 'head' and 'girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nutmeg is the aromatic seed of an East Indies tree, ground as a cooking flavouring.

clue.text: Every man over forty is a Shaw's Man and Superman

definitions.text: Every man over forty is a Shaw's Man and Superman

parts.words: Every man over forty is a Shaw's Man and Superman
parts.note: a quotation from George Bernard Shaw's Maxims for Revolutionists, appended to his play Man and Superman; the missing last word of the saying is the entry

explanation.surface: A line from a Shaw play about middle-aged men.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw's maxim reads in full 'Every man over forty is a scoundrel'; the clue gives the quotation with its last word missing and names the source.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's saying names a rogue or villain as the thing every middle-aged man becomes.

clue.text: A restorative, no matter how taken

indicators.note: the word reads the same whichever way it is taken, from the front or from the back

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A tonic that works however you swallow it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No matter how taken' sounds like dosage advice, but it means the word is a palindrome, the same read forwards or backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that revives, such as a stiff drink or tonic, brings a person back to vigour.

clue.text: Crete isn't perhaps to be split in two

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of these words might be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: A question of whether the island of Crete should be divided.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals rearranging the letters of CRETE and ISNT.
explanation.definitionFit: To intersect is to cut across something, dividing it into two parts.

clue.text: Spotted a French heel accepting a note

indicators.note: taking something in, so the note goes inside the other letters

parts.note: un is French for a
a ship heels when it leans or lists to one side
C is a musical note

explanation.surface: A grubby French cad who has taken a banknote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heel' wants to be a cad, but here it is the ship's verb, to lean. C goes between UN and LEAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Spotted in the sense of soiled or stained, dirty, morally or physically.

clue.text: Second to finish and awfully sore!

parts.note: end means finish, as in to end or finish something

indicators.note: awfully suggests the letters are badly jumbled

explanation.surface: Coming second in a race and feeling terribly sore afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like a race position, but it is the verb, to back a proposal. 'awfully' turns SORE into ORSE after END.
explanation.definitionFit: To second a motion is to support or back it, as one does when approving or signing off.

clue.text: The man locating pests around a city in years gone by

indicators.note: the pests surround what follows, so the city goes inside them

parts.note: mice are household pests
Ur was an ancient Sumerian city in Mesopotamia

explanation.surface: A man who finds vermin round an old city.
explanation.walkthrough: A and UR go inside MICE: M-AUR-ICE. Ur, in modern Iraq, is the crossword's usual ancient city.
explanation.definitionFit: Maurice is a man's first name, so any bearer is a male person.

clue.text: What a person requires for the shoot is transport and backbone

definitions.text: What a person requires for the shoot

parts.note: a cart is a means of transport
a ridge is a long spine-like crest, as of a roof or hill

explanation.surface: A shooting party member needs a vehicle and some courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backbone' suggests courage, but here it is a ridge. A shoot is a hunting party, needing ammunition.
explanation.definitionFit: A gun needs a casing of shot and powder to fire, essential kit on a game-shooting day.

clue.text: The gods seen by 26?

parts.note: in theatre slang the gods are the highest, cheapest seats, which a performer on stage looks up at

explanation.surface: Deities appearing before a performer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The gods' suggests deities, but it is theatre slang for the top tier of seats, which an actress (26) sees from the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper balcony of a theatre is nicknamed the gods because it is nearest heaven.

clue.text: Needs gas fitting, being very old

indicators.note: fitting as in installing a gas supply, putting the letters into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: An old house needs a gas supply installed because it is so ancient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fitting' looks like plumbing work but signals rearranging NEEDS and GAS.
explanation.definitionFit: Agedness is the state of advanced years, great age.

clue.text: For the Left, pictures backing of stars

parts.note: for can mean as, in the role of, as in taking someone for or as a fool

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word for pictures is read in reverse

parts.note: art means pictures collectively
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Left-wing cinema films supporting celebrity actors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' looks like political support for the Left, but it turns ART round to TRA.
explanation.definitionFit: Astral means relating to the heavenly bodies, celestial, starry.

clue.text: Wanting the lot on tick is quite OK

parts.note: all means the lot, everything
on tick is British slang for on credit, so able to be owed

explanation.surface: Someone who wants everything on credit insists it is perfectly acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanting' sets the surface: the whole lot being owable. ON TICK is British slang for on credit.
explanation.definitionFit: Something permissible is acceptable, within the rules.

clue.text: The supporters present in a new stand

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other
new suggests the letters of stand in a fresh arrangement

parts.note: here means present, in attendance

explanation.surface: The fans are in attendance in a recently built stand at the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' turns STAND into DNTS, and 'in' puts HERE inside it after D, with A in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Followers or backers of a cause or party are its loyal following.

clue.text: This is the last month many are to publish

parts.note: Dec is the short form of December, the last month of the year
L is the Roman numeral fifty, a crossword stand-in for many

explanation.surface: In December, lots of people will release their work.
explanation.definitionFit: To declare is to announce or make known publicly.

clue.text: Having a salesman come inside he'll be sorry!

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative
to enter is to come in

explanation.surface: Inviting a door-to-door salesman in, a man will live to regret it.
explanation.walkthrough: A REPENTER is one who repents, so 'he'll be sorry' stands for the person.
explanation.definitionFit: One who feels remorse for wrongdoing is a penitent person.

clue.text: Writers must pay the price

parts.note: reads as a warning that authors suffer, but the letter-writer literally pays the cost of sending mail

explanation.surface: Authors must suffer for their art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pay the price' suggests suffering consequences; read literally it is the cost of sending letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The fee charged for sending a letter by mail is what letter writers pay.

clue.text: Some juniors shield esteemed senior

indicators.note: some of the letters of these words, taken as a run from within them

explanation.surface: Younger pupils protect a well-respected older pupil.
explanation.definitionFit: The oldest child of a family is the senior one by age.

clue.text: Knights holding acknowledgement of indebtedness ar suspect

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the second piece goes inside the first

parts.note: to dub someone is to make them a knight by touching the shoulder with a sword
an IOU, I owe you, is a written note acknowledging a debt

explanation.surface: Noble knights in debt are not to be trusted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knights' reads as noblemen, but it is the verb, makes into a knight, giving DUBS.
explanation.definitionFit: Dubious means doubtful, questionable, open to suspicion.

clue.text: Certain to keep the retired fellow in style

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it within, so the second piece is put inside

parts.note: sure means certain

indicators.note: retired means drawn back, so the word for fellow is read backwards

parts.note: man means fellow, chap

explanation.surface: A pensioner sure to live comfortably.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' turns MAN into NAM, which goes inside SURE between R and E. 'Style' is a verb, to name or call.
explanation.definitionFit: Style as a noun is a title or name by which someone is known, such as a family name.

clue.text: The taker of the long-distance record

definitions.text: The taker of the long-distance record

parts.words: The taker of the long-distance record
parts.note: sounds like a champion runner, but means an instrument that records the miles travelled

explanation.surface: An athlete who set the record for a long race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taker of the record' suggests a champion, but the device takes (measures) distances.
explanation.definitionFit: The dashboard gauge counting a vehicle's total mileage measures distance covered.

clue.text: S2 Spring

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'S2 Spring (6)': 'S2' is an OCR garble of the printed clue and no source gives the wordplay for EASTER.

clue.text: Place where one may get busy early

indicators.note: suggests the letters of the following words may be got into a different order

explanation.surface: A spot where people tend to get busy first thing.
explanation.walkthrough: AYLESBURY is the county town of Buckinghamshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Aylesbury is a town in Buckinghamshire, an example of a location.

clue.text: A number with long hair will take part

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the person who takes a part in a play

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral one hundred
a tress is a long lock of hair

explanation.surface: A singer with flowing locks will join in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A number' looks like a song, but A and C (100) are separate. The definition describes what a performer does, taking a role.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman performer plays a role in a stage show or film.

clue.text: Seating a Turk

definitions.meaning: a low padded seat or footstool without a back
a native of the old Turkish empire ruled from Constantinople

explanation.definitionFit: The word names both an upholstered seat and a subject of the Turkish empire.

clue.text: The heir is accorded an entry in general

indicators.note: one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: Robert E Lee was the commanding general of the Confederate army
a gate is a way in, an entry

explanation.surface: A will's beneficiary is given a mention in an overall listing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in general' looks like a phrase meaning broadly, but GATE goes into LEE, the American Civil War general.
explanation.definitionFit: One who receives a bequest under a will inherits from the deceased.

clue.text: Subdued yet again by newspaper leader

parts.note: re- is a prefix meaning again
the press means newspapers
ED, editor, is the person who writes a newspaper's leader column

explanation.surface: Crushed once more by an editorial.
explanation.definitionFit: Repressed means held down, restrained, kept in check.
